```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
set.seed(1)
```

```{r setup}
library(koine)
```

## What koine does

koine synthesises *one* coherent, independent predictive opinion for a Bayesian
model from a curated battery of inference lenses --- or it abstains when no
diversity gain exists. It stacks over model-structure and method diversity in
predictive space, on an axis orthogonal to any panel of inference engines it
sits beside. This vignette walks the increment-1 spine: the request, the
battery, one lens, and the synthesis-or-abstain decision.

## The request: a `pass`

A `pass` is an engine-neutral, declarative request. It carries the formula, the
data, an evaluable family, the canonical observation axis, and a content hash.

```{r pass}
set.seed(42)
n <- 40L
x <- rnorm(n)
d <- data.frame(y = 1.5 + 0.8 * x + rnorm(n, sd = 0.7), x = x)

pass <- koine_pass(y ~ x, data = d, family = gaussian())
pass
```

The family is wrapped into an *evaluable* `family_spec`: koine computes the
pointwise log-likelihood itself, because the upstream family object exposes a
mean function but no log-likelihood.

```{r family}
fs <- as_family_spec(gaussian())
fs$loglik_pointwise(y = c(0, 1), eta = c(0, 1), aux = list(sigma = 1))
```

## The battery

`resolve_battery()` enrols only the lenses whose family, features, and tier fit
the request --- and records *why* each excluded lens was left out. Honest,
logged absence is the rule; silent omission is never allowed.

```{r resolve}
res <- resolve_battery(pass)
vapply(res$enrolled, function(L) L$id, character(1))
res$excluded
```

For this Gaussian model several lenses resolve --- DRAM, NIMBLE-Gibbs and DREAM
(different inference families on the same posterior), plus the model-structure
variants: robust-t and a shrinkage spectrum (ridge, lasso, horseshoe). The
Polya-Gamma Gibbs lens is excluded on family grounds (it serves binomial
logistic models, not Gaussian), and that exclusion carries its reason.

## One lens: delayed-rejection adaptive Metropolis

```{r dram}
fit <- fit_dram(pass, n_iter = 1500L, n_burn = 750L, n_chains = 2L)
fit
posterior::summarise_draws(fit$draws, "mean", "sd")
```

The estimated intercept and slope recover the data-generating `1.5` and `0.8`.

## Synthesis: realising diversity

koine's value as a fourth witness comes from *diversity*. Lenses that fit the
same model only corroborate one another --- a useful consistency check, but the
stacking weights then collapse onto a single component. Genuine diversity needs
a different model *structure*. The robust-t lens supplies one: a Student-t
likelihood whose heavy tails give a materially different predictive when the
data depart from Gaussianity.

```{r synthesise}
set.seed(7)
xd <- rnorm(150)
yd <- 1 + 0.8 * xd + rt(150, df = 5) * 0.6        # moderately heavy-tailed
pass_ht <- koine_pass(yd ~ xd, data.frame(yd = yd, xd = xd), gaussian())

reg <- koine_stage1_registry()
bid <- function(id) which(vapply(reg, function(z) z$id, "") == id)
reg2 <- list(reg[[bid("dram")]], reg[[bid("robust_t")]])
reg2[[1]]$fit_fn <- function(p, ls) fit_dram(p, ls, 2000L, 1000L, 2L)
reg2[[2]]$fit_fn <- function(p, ls) fit_robust_t(p, ls, nu = 4, n_iter = 2000L,
                                                 n_burn = 1000L, n_chains = 2L)

res <- synthesise(pass_ht, registry = reg2)
res
res$independence[, c("lens_id", "family", "kernel")]
```

The weights do not collapse: the Gaussian (DRAM) and Student-t lenses each carry
real weight, and the diversity diagnostic reports more than one effective
component. That spread is the orthogonal-diversity signal --- the fourth opinion
is sensitive to model structure, not a weighted echo of a single posterior.

## Mixed models: a random intercept

koine also handles a single random intercept, `(1 | g)`. The opinion is built on
an axis orthogonal to the sealed engines: NIMBLE-Gibbs (`fit_nimble_glmm()`)
*samples* the random effects, while the marginal lens (`fit_glmm_marginal()`,
shown here because it needs no extra toolchain) *integrates* them out --- exactly
for the Gaussian LMM, by adaptive Gauss-Hermite quadrature for the binomial GLMM.
Both report `(beta, sigma, tau)` and are stacked on the same per-observation
*integrated* predictive (the random effect marginalised under each draw's
variance components), which keeps the leave-one-out gate reliable. (A Poisson
GLMM path exists but is held experimental pending a better-mixing sampler.)

```{r re}
set.seed(20)
g <- factor(rep(1:25, each = 6))
xr <- rnorm(150)
b <- rnorm(25, 0, 1.1)                              # group random intercepts
yr <- 1 + 0.5 * xr + b[g] + rnorm(150, 0, 0.7)
pass_re <- koine_pass(yr ~ xr + (1 | g),
                      data.frame(yr = yr, xr = xr, g = g), gaussian())

fit_re <- fit_glmm_marginal(pass_re, n_iter = 2000L, n_burn = 1000L,
                            n_chains = 2L)
posterior::summarise_draws(fit_re$draws, "mean")    # recovers beta, sigma, tau
```

A third lens, `fit_glmm_robust_re()`, gives the random intercepts heavy
(Student-t) tails. Where the two Gaussian-RE lenses corroborate (their weights
collapse), this structure variant earns real stacking weight when group effects
are outlying --- so koine's mixed-model opinion, like its population battery,
becomes sensitive to model structure rather than a weighted echo of one
assumption.

## Multi-environment trials: variety and trial together

The breeder-standard multi-environment-trial (MET) model carries *two* random
intercepts --- a variety effect and a trial (environment) effect, crossed (each
variety grown across many trials) or nested. koine fits this structure directly
with `(1 | variety) + (1 | trial)`, so it corroborates a production MET model on
the model that model actually fits, not on a single-random-effect reduction that
discards the trial structure. The Gaussian MET marginal stays exact: the random
effects are integrated out through a dense Cholesky of `V = sigma^2 I +
tau_variety^2 Z_variety Z_variety' + tau_trial^2 Z_trial Z_trial'`, where the
sealed engines instead sample (NIMBLE) or Laplace-approximate (INLA) them.

```{r met}
set.seed(404)
nv <- 16L                                          # varieties
nt <- 8L                                           # trials (environments)
u <- rnorm(nv, 0, 1.0)                             # variety effects
v <- rnorm(nt, 0, 2.5)                             # trial effects (dominant)
rows <- list()
for (i in seq_len(nv)) {
  trials_i <- sample(seq_len(nt), 5L)             # an incomplete (unbalanced) MET
  for (t in trials_i) {
    rows[[length(rows) + 1L]] <- data.frame(
      variety = i, trial = t,
      yield = 5 + u[i] + v[t] + rnorm(1L, 0, 0.6))
  }
}
met <- do.call(rbind, rows)
met$variety <- factor(met$variety)
met$trial <- factor(met$trial)

pass_met <- koine_pass(yield ~ 1 + (1 | variety) + (1 | trial), met, gaussian(),
                       seed = 5L)
pass_met                                           # tagged [MET], crossed
fit_met <- fit_glmm_marginal(pass_met, n_iter = 1500L, n_burn = 750L,
                             n_chains = 2L)
posterior::summarise_draws(fit_met$draws, "mean")  # b0, sigma, tau_variety, tau_trial
```

The draws now carry one `tau_<grouping>` per random factor. koine's MET variety
effects corroborate the production MET model (here `lme4`, fitted by REML)
faithfully, and far more so than the single-random-intercept reduction --- which,
on an unbalanced trial with a dominant environment effect, confounds each
variety with the trials it happened to be grown in.

```{r met-corroborate, eval = requireNamespace("lme4", quietly = TRUE)}
prod <- lme4::lmer(yield ~ 1 + (1 | variety) + (1 | trial), met, REML = TRUE)
blup_met <- lme4::ranef(prod)$variety[, 1]
single <- lme4::lmer(yield ~ 1 + (1 | variety), met, REML = TRUE)
blup_single <- lme4::ranef(single)$variety[, 1]

# koine MET variety effects (GLS BLUP at the posterior-mean variance components)
sm <- posterior::summarise_draws(fit_met$draws, "mean")
mv <- stats::setNames(sm$mean, sm$variable)
design <- koine:::.pass_design(pass_met)
red <- koine:::.pass_re_design(pass_met)
taus <- c(mv["tau_variety"], mv["tau_trial"])
v_mat <- koine:::.re_marginal_cov(design$N, red$factors, taus, mv["sigma"])
resid <- design$y - as.numeric(design$X %*% mv[paste0("b_", colnames(design$X))])
z_var <- koine:::.re_indicator(red$factors[[1L]]$group, red$factors[[1L]]$n_groups)
u_koine <- as.numeric(taus[1L]^2 * t(z_var) %*% solve(v_mat, resid))

c(koine_MET_vs_production = cor(u_koine, blup_met),
  single_RE_vs_production = cor(blup_single, blup_met))
```

A non-Gaussian MET --- whose dense crossed marginal has no exact quadrature ---
is declined honestly rather than approximated:

```{r met-glmm-abstain}
counts <- transform(met, n = rpois(nrow(met), 4))
fit_glmm_marginal(koine_pass(n ~ 1 + (1 | variety) + (1 | trial), counts,
                             poisson()))$reason
```

Richer structure is refused rather than fitted as the wrong model: a random
slope, or more than two grouping factors, makes koine abstain
`feature_unsupported`.

```{r re-abstain}
pass_bad <- koine_pass(yr ~ xr + (xr | g),
                       data.frame(yr = yr, xr = xr, g = g), gaussian())
synthesise(pass_bad)$reason
```

## When koine abstains

Abstention is a first-class outcome, not an error. If fewer than two
independent opinion lenses resolve --- for instance with a single-lens battery
--- koine declines to guess and says why.

```{r abstain}
out <- synthesise(pass, registry = list(koine_stage1_registry()[[1]]))
is_abstention(out)
out
```

Under-claiming beats a wrong fourth opinion: that is the design intent.
